content:
There was a proverb I came across once that’s stuck with me: “If brothers were such a good idea, God would have given himself one.” Harsh, but not untrue. At least as far back as Cain and Abel, the relationship between brothers has proved to be a complicated one, full of petty resentments, jealousies, and competition—but also the unique understanding that only brothers can have, like magnets with the same charge: alike, and therefore repulsed by each other.

If brotherhood can be a burden, it’s especially so for the younger brother. He comes into the world already being measured against the yardstick of his older brother’s accomplishments, often destined by birth order to live in the shadow of a favored firstborn. It leaves him with one of two options: to follow in his older brother’s footsteps without hope of living up to expectations, or to rebel, branching out on his own path to the inevitable disappointment of parents who wish he could be more like his brother.

My novel Men Like Us explores this dynamic through the Kennedy family. Bobby Kennedy occupies the shaky ground of the younger brother, torn between the pressure to live up to his charming older brother Jack while at the same time trying to develop his own identity independent of his sibling. I wanted to explore what it felt like to be caught between two competing impulses, what it was like to be the “spare,” not the heir, and the expectations and challenges that might come with living your life in the wings instead of on center stage.

For all its faults, the bond between brothers, or any siblings, is the true cradle-to-grave relationship—just as important, in my opinion, as any of the more commonly depicted bonds in literature, between romantic partners or parents and children. Equal parts fraught and exhilarating, brotherhood is a relationship like no other, someone you don’t choose but have to travel alongside through life nonetheless. In the seven kitaplar below, we see a variety of brothers and permutations of this thorny relationship—some younger brothers who look up to the older, some who want nothing to do with them, all inextricably bonded to a person who understands them (or doesn’t) like no one else in the world.

Although ostensibly a queer Romeo and Juliet set in a Glasgow government housing scheme, Young Mungo is also a story about brothers. In Mungo’s world, Protestant and Catholic gangs are at war with each other. Though he has no taste for violence himself, Mungo’s older brother Hamish serves as the leader and general of one of the Protestant gangs. The two brothers are opposites: Mungo is sweet, emotionally perceptive, tender. By contrast, Hamish thinks with his fists, embodying the brash, violent masculinity their world demands for survival. Throughout the novel, Hamish tries to coach Mungo into being more like him, pulling Mungo deeper into gang politics even as Mungo is simultaneously falling for a Catholic boy who lives in the same housing scheme. By the end, the question isn’t whether Mungo will ever be able to follow in his brother’s footsteps, but exactly what it will cost him to do so.

Salvage the Bones follows siblings Randall, Skeetah, Esch, and Junior as they prepare for Hurricane Katrina in their rural Mississippi town. Although the novel juggles multiple threads, including the coming storm and Esch’s unexpected pregnancy, one of the most compelling arcs for me centers on Skeetah—the second son—and his place within the family. While his older brother Randall is a talented basketball player whose skill offers a possible route out of their town, Skeetah devotes himself to a completely different path with the same intensity: pitbull fighting. With the two, Ward captures the subtle tension that can exist between younger and older brothers—less an outright, declared rivalry than an unspoken attempt by the younger brother to carve out a unique identity for himself. The result is an understated but no less powerful example of how birth order can shape the identities of brothers themselves.

Following two brothers in the wake of their father’s death, Intermezzo maps the contentious relationship between younger brother Ivan and older brother Peter as they navigate their grief amidst a lifetime of accumulated misunderstandings. While many kitaplar explore the relationship between brothers in childhood, what appeals to me most about this novel is that it spotlights how the sibling relationship evolves—sometimes awkwardly—into adulthood, when the hierarchy established in childhood no longer fits. Peter remains convinced he knows what’s best for Ivan and what “normal” adult life should look like; Ivan resents Peter’s interference and judgement of him. Through Ivan, the book captures the growing pains of being the younger brother and the difficulty of trying to establish your own life while still being seen through the eyes of an older brother who’ll always see you as a child.

This novel is perfect for anyone with a Western itch to scratch. Assassin brothers Eli and Charlie Sisters are sent by their boss to kill a prospector on his gold mining claim. Along the way, Eli (the younger of the two) begins to question his life as a hitman, a concern that his more aggressive, less introspective brother doesn’t share. The novel tracks their journey (and Eli’s growing doubts) through a series of absurd detours that give the story a picaresque, episodic feel from chapter to chapter. As with Intermezzo, the novel explores what happens when two brothers start to diverge—as well as the bonds between them that, try as they might, can never be severed completely.

content:
As you might imagine, we read a lot of kitaplar here at EL. Followers of our Instagram may be familiar with our long-running What We’re Reading series, where we post every other week about what staff members have been reading and loving. Recently, we decided it was time to make this tradition a little more special, and asked staff and interns to share a few thoughts on the kitaplar that have been lingering on their nightstands. Below are the titles our team read over the summer—old and new—that excited them the most.

I was in New York on a day when wildfire smoke had settled over the city. Breathing the air, they told us, was like smoking a pack of cigarettes. Needing to be transported somewhere far away, I read Aguda’s strange and beautiful novel. It is set in Lagos (far enough!), a city that is rendered in all its contradictions, chaos, and vitality. Instead of offering escape, the novel reminded me that cities, however different, ask the same impossible thing of us: to build lives alongside one another while the ground beneath us is constantly shifting.

I had so much fun reading this whip-fast story of a Singaporean criminal on the run, told in podcast form. As someone who loves the idea of podcasts but is a much better reader than listener, this was perfect for me: all the voice and personality a podcast offers, but on the page instead! I was drawn right in by the narrator’s delightfully irreverent voice and couldn’t stop hitting play on the next episode.

J Brooke’s debut poetry collection is an incredibly candid look at what it means to be queer in so many contexts: what it means to be part of a family, both of origin and chosen. What it means to move actively in a society that often won’t protect you; what it means to parent a queer child; and what it means to be doing all of this right now, in this version of America. This collection is whip-smart, bursting with heart, and generous with its humor. It’s a quick read, but I loved every second of it.

I’ve always had a complicated relationship with mentorship. What happens if you tether yourself to a mentor who, ultimately, isn’t who you imagined them to be? This question is at the heart of Famous Men, one Buntin’s protagonist, Will, must navigate on her own. The result is an unflinching portrait of power dynamics, ambition, desires of all kinds, and what happens when a mentor’s voice looms large over your writing and your life—even when you want to escape it. Compelling, gorgeously written, and complex in all the best ways.

Feldman captures a hot, sticky, teenage summer in the suburbs with discerning, literary prose and picture-perfect intensity. The protagonist of Meg Mason’s new book, the follow-up to the 2020 tragicomedy Sorrow and Bliss, is an invisible woman. She might well be standing there but you won’t notice her. She’s a techie at literary festivals – the person who shuffles up to a famous writer a few minutes before their event and apologetically slides a microphone cable down their shirt while they’re making small talk with the chair or accepting a bottle of room-temperature mineral water from an anxious publicist.

No man is a hero to his valet, and no writer is a hero to the technical staff lurking in the wings of a venue. Mason’s opening pages present a teasing but not quite libellous series of cameos from real writers: George Saunders deciding at an inconsiderately late stage to insist on swapping his headset for a lapel mic; Ann Patchett being frosty with a fan; Mick Herron accidentally stepping on someone’s foot and not apologising.

Uluslararası Edebiyat Seçkisi: Ghadeer Bustani, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.... (The Paris Review editoryal arşivinden Türkçeye uyarlanmıştır.)

In 1677, a medical student named Johann Ham approached the Dutch scientist and future “Father of Microbiology” Antonie van Leeuwenhoek with unsettling news: there were tiny creatures living in his semen. Or not in his semen, not necessarily. Some incorrigible friend—someone who certainly wasn’t Ham—had dislodged his wad in the company of an “unclean woman” and then transferred custody of his deposit by means unattested into Ham’s hands. Curious Ham had splashed the discharge under a microscope and, startled by its contents, brought his discovery and its medium to Van Leeuwenhoek for a second opinion. Examining the sample, the renowned microscopist, who had already described what we call red blood cells and protists in pioneering detail, glimpsed spindly tailed animalcules moving in the muck. He proceeded to set about procuring new goo from a close, morally uncompromised source. “What I here describe was not obtained by any sinful contrivance on my part, but the observations were made upon the excess with which Nature provided me in my conjugal relations,” he wrote some months later to the Royal Society of London regarding the remains of an emission he’d slathered under his powerful single-lens microscope.

I relate this lightly editorialized and moderately abridged history of the identification of what would become known as spermatozoa because it marks the first time that a man had cause and the capability to wonder at the meaning of the living contents of his ejaculate—and thus to search his little reflecting pool for the secrets of humanity, of himself. And because, in 2024, some 347 years after Van Leeuwenhoek fired his fateful blast, a money-minded form of this fascination prompted a team of teenage and early-twenties shitpost entrepreneurs in Silicon Valley to found a sports start-up called Sperm Racing. It has raised $10 million in funding.

The company first came to my attention this February, a month before it was due to roll out an ambitious Sperm Racing World Cup featuring contestants representing 128 countries. When an editor for this magazine asked me to write about the championship, I began to picture myself as an anxious, anthropomorphized gamete paddling desperately toward its subject, its theme, its egg, endeavoring to fulfill its purpose, to conceive a story. Come is, as it happens, a subject on which I enjoy some expertise. Through the power of the internet and promiscuity, I’ve learned to appreciate the rich diversity of whitish matter the human body can produce. Color, velocity, viscosity, volume, reach, and duration differ from person to person, from shot to shot. I’ve become familiar with the venerable tradition, staged between men (and not only men) every day, of exhibition, comparison, and analysis, in which the relation between the two parties, or between one’s fantasy and one’s reality, or between one’s present output and one’s memory of past productions, adds to the pleasure that inheres in the act itself.

Sperm Racing is, more or less, a scientized and de-eroticized update on this “venerable tradition.” At the Sperm Racing headquarters in San Francisco, two contestants donate their semen, which is centrifugally cleaned; healthy sperm are isolated from the samples; and the cells then race through courses less than a half-centimeter long that are etched into microfluidic silicon chips. The sperm are pipetted into warm liquid currents designed to mimic the reproductive environment; these currents allow the cells to orient themselves in the faux canal, such that the cells begin to swim upstream, as they would against the flow of mucus in a vagina, toward the finish line. (Until recently, the company’s chief science officer was a teenager named Rishi Kanaparti, whose past work includes papers on, among other things, “Motion Resilient Deep Learning for ECG Signal Classification.”) The raw footage is boring and difficult for the human eye to parse—vaguely defined blobs move against a white background—so the company’s computers track the cells’ coordinates and generate visual approximations of the contests. They then debut these videos at occasional live events, like one that pitted a USC student against a UCLA student last April, and post them on social media. Several Reels on Instagram feature a bellowing commentator who goes by BSTCHLD. “This is a microscopic masterclass,” BSTCHLD shouts during one blowout. As a sperm enters the end zone: “INSEMINATION!”

One such plan: In the spirit of participatory journalism, I applied to the Sperm Racing World Cup a few days after receiving this assignment, assuming that I would be screened out for being old (thirty-three), common (American), and of no particular repute as a content creator and thus of no particular value to a would-be sport whose founders require significant reserves of the public’s attention for their goop regatta saga to succeed. I answered questions about my ancestry, diet, workout frequency and routine, and motivations (options included “fertility awareness” and “national pride”). I dutifully took screenshots of the Sperm Racing webpage and forwarded them to my editor. I scoured my inbox for a form email explaining my unworthiness—“Do Not Come,” its subject line might have read—but found nothing. I waited.
